prompt:
(a) Suppose that each square of a $4\times 7$ chessboard, as shown in the figure, is colored either black or white. Prove that with any such coloring, the board must contain a rectangle (formed by the horizontal and vertical lines of the board such as the one outlined in the figure) whose four distinct unit corner squares are all of the same color.

(b) Exhibit a black-white coloring of a $4\times 6$ board in which the four corner squares of every rectangle, as described above, are not all of the same color.
answer: (a) Each column has at least $2$ monochromatic (row-pair, colour) combinations, giving $\ge 14 > 6\cdot 2 = 12$, so two columns share one. (b) Use the six different columns with exactly two black squares.

solutions.title: Pigeonhole on pairs of rows
solutions.body:
**(a)** A monochromatic rectangle is the same as two columns and two rows such that both columns have the same colour in both of these rows. For each column, call a pair of rows together with a colour a *mono-pair* of the column if the column has that colour in both rows.

A column with $k$ black and $4-k$ white squares has $\binom k2 + \binom{4-k}2$ mono-pairs; for $k = 0,1,2,3,4$ this is $6, 3, 2, 3, 6$, so always at least $2$. The $7$ columns therefore have at least $14$ mono-pairs in total. But there are only $\binom42\cdot 2 = 12$ possible (pair of rows, colour) combinations. By the pigeonhole principle, two different columns have the same mono-pair: the same colour in the same two rows. These two columns and two rows form a rectangle with four corners of one colour. ∎

**(b)** Use the six columns that contain exactly two black squares, each pattern once (rows listed top to bottom, B = black, W = white):
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} & 1&2&3&4&5&6\\ \hline \text{row }1 & B&B&B&W&W&W\\ \text{row }2 & B&W&W&B&B&W\\ \text{row }3 & W&B&W&B&W&B\\ \text{row }4 & W&W&B&W&B&B\end{array}$$
Suppose two columns had the same colour in the same two rows. If that colour is black, the two black squares of each column are exactly in these two rows, so the two columns have the same pattern — but all six columns are different. If it is white, the same argument applies to the two white squares. So no rectangle has four corners of the same colour.

prompt: If $A$ and $B$ are fixed points on a given circle and $XY$ is a variable diameter of the same circle, determine the locus of the point of intersection of lines $AX$ and $BY$. You may assume that $AB$ is not a diameter.
answer: The circle through $A$ and $B$ whose center is the intersection $T$ of the tangents at $A$ and $B$ (it is orthogonal to the given circle) — except for the two points of it diametrically opposite $A$ and $B$, which correspond to the excluded positions $X=A$ and $Y=B$.

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Take the given circle $\Gamma$ to be the unit circle and place $A = (-a, b)$, $B = (a,b)$ with $a > 0$, $a^2+b^2 = 1$. Since $AB$ is not a diameter, $b\ne 0$; by reflecting we may assume $b>0$. Let $X = (r,s)$ and $Y = (-r,-s)$ with $r^2+s^2=1$. The lines $AX$, $BY$ are defined when $X\neq A$ and $Y \ne B$, i.e. $X\notin\{A, -B\}$.

**The candidate point.** Let
$$P = \left(\frac{as}{b},\ \frac{1-ar}{b}\right).$$
$P$ lies on line $AX$: using $1-b^2 = a^2$,
$$(r+a)\Big(\tfrac{1-ar}{b}-b\Big) - (s-b)\Big(\tfrac{as}{b}+a\Big) = \tfrac{a}{b}\big[(r+a)(a-r) - (s-b)(s+b)\big] = \tfrac ab\big[a^2+b^2 - r^2 - s^2\big] = 0.$$
Similarly $P$ lies on line $BY$:
$$(-r-a)\Big(\tfrac{1-ar}{b}-b\Big) + (s+b)\Big(\tfrac{as}{b}-a\Big) = \tfrac ab\big[-(a^2-r^2) + s^2-b^2\big] = 0.$$
The lines $AX$ and $BY$ are distinct (otherwise the four points $A,X,B,Y$ of $\Gamma$ would be collinear, forcing $\{A,X\} = \{B,Y\}$, i.e. $X = B$, $Y = A$ and $AB$ a diameter). Two distinct lines through a common point meet only there, so $P$ is *the* intersection point of $AX$ and $BY$.

**The locus.** The map $(r,s)\mapsto\left(\frac{as}{b},\frac{1-ar}{b}\right)$ is an invertible affine map, with inverse $r = \frac{1-by}{a}$, $s = \frac{bx}a$. So $(x,y)$ is an image point iff
$$\Big(\frac{bx}{a}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{1-by}{a}\Big)^2 = 1 \iff x^2 + \Big(y - \frac1b\Big)^2 = \frac{a^2}{b^2},$$
using $a^2+b^2=1$. This is the circle $\omega$ with center $T = (0, 1/b)$ and radius $a/b$. It passes through $A$ and $B$ (e.g. $a^2 + (b-\frac1b)^2 = \frac{(1-b^2)^2}{b^2} + a^2 = \frac{a^4 + a^2b^2}{b^2} = \frac{a^2}{b^2}$), and $T$ is where the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $A$ and $B$ meet (the tangent at $B$ is $ax+by = 1$, which hits the $y$-axis at $1/b$). Also $TA^2 + OA^2 = \frac{a^2}{b^2}+1 = \frac{1}{b^2} = OT^2$, so $\omega$ is orthogonal to $\Gamma$.

**Excluded points.** As $X$ runs over all of $\Gamma$, $P$ runs over all of $\omega$. The two excluded positions are $X = A$, giving $(a, \frac{1+a^2}{b}) = 2T - A$, and $X = -B$, giving $(-a,\frac{1+a^2}b) = 2T-B$: the points of $\omega$ diametrically opposite $A$ and $B$. (If one takes the line "$AX$" for $X = A$ to be the tangent at $A$, these points are obtained too.)

**Answer:** the locus is the circle through $A$ and $B$ centered at the intersection of the tangents to the given circle at $A$ and $B$, without the two points diametrically opposite $A$ and $B$ on it.

solutions.title: Modulo 4 and infinite descent
solutions.body:
Squares are $\equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$, with $x^2\equiv 0$ iff $x$ is even.

**Claim.** If integers satisfy $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 4^m a^2b^2$ for some $m\ge 0$, then $a, b, c$ are all even, and $(a/2, b/2, c/2)$ satisfies the same equation with $m+1$.

*Proof.* If $m\ge 1$, the right side is $\equiv 0 \pmod 4$. A sum of three squares is $\equiv 0 \pmod 4$ only if all three squares are $\equiv 0$, so $a,b,c$ are even.

If $m = 0$: if $a$ and $b$ are both odd, the right side is $\equiv 1$ while the left is $1 + 1 + c^2 \equiv 2$ or $3 \pmod 4$. If exactly one of $a, b$ is odd, the right side is $\equiv 0$ and the left is $1 + 0 + c^2\equiv 1$ or $2$. So $a, b$ are even; then the right side is $\equiv 0\pmod 4$, and $c^2 \equiv 0$, so $c$ is even too.

Finally, substituting $a = 2a_1$, $b = 2b_1$, $c = 2c_1$ gives $4(a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2) = 4^m\cdot 16\,a_1^2b_1^2$, i.e. $a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2 = 4^{m+1}a_1^2b_1^2$. $\square$

Starting from a solution of $a^2+b^2+c^2 = a^2b^2$ (the case $m = 0$) and applying the claim repeatedly, $a, b, c$ are divisible by $2^k$ for every $k$. The only such integer is $0$. Conversely $(0,0,0)$ is a solution.

**Answer:** $(a,b,c) = (0,0,0)$ only. ∎

prompt: If the sum of the lengths of the six edges of a trirectangular tetrahedron $PABC$ (i.e., $\angle APB=\angle BPC=\angle CPA=90^\circ$) is $S$, determine its maximum volume.

solutions.title: Two AM–GM steps
solutions.body:
Let $PA = a$, $PB = b$, $PC = c$. The other edges are $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, $\sqrt{b^2+c^2}$, $\sqrt{c^2+a^2}$, and the volume is $V = \frac{abc}{6}$ (the right angles at $P$ make $PC$ the height over the right triangle $PAB$).

By AM–GM, $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\ge\sqrt{2ab}$, etc., and then
$$S = (a+b+c) + \big(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}+\sqrt{b^2+c^2}+\sqrt{c^2+a^2}\big) \ge 3\sqrt[3]{abc} + \sqrt2\big(\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{bc}+\sqrt{ca}\big) \ge 3\sqrt[3]{abc} + 3\sqrt2\,\sqrt[3]{abc},$$
using AM–GM on $\sqrt{ab},\sqrt{bc},\sqrt{ca}$ (whose product is $abc$). Hence
$$\sqrt[3]{abc} \le \frac{S}{3(1+\sqrt2)} = \frac{(\sqrt2-1)S}{3},\qquad V = \frac{abc}6\le \frac{(\sqrt2-1)^3S^3}{162}.$$
All the AM–GM steps are equalities when $a = b = c$; then $S = 3a(1+\sqrt2)$, i.e. $a = \frac{(\sqrt2-1)S}{3}$, and $V = \frac{a^3}{6}$ equals the bound.

**Answer:** the maximum volume is $\dfrac{(\sqrt2-1)^3S^3}{162} = \dfrac{(5\sqrt2-7)S^3}{162}$.

prompt:
If $P(x)$, $Q(x)$, $R(x)$, and $S(x)$ are all polynomials such that
$$P(x^5) + xQ(x^5) + x^2 R(x^5) = (x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x +1) S(x),$$
prove that $x-1$ is a factor of $P(x)$.
answer: Substitute the four primitive fifth roots of unity: $P(1)+\omega Q(1)+\omega^2R(1)=0$ for four distinct $\omega$, so the quadratic $P(1)+Q(1)t+R(1)t^2$ is identically zero; in particular $P(1)=0$.

solutions.title: Plug in fifth roots of unity
solutions.body:
Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/5}$. For $k = 1,2,3,4$, the number $\omega^k$ satisfies $(\omega^k)^5 = 1$ and $\omega^k\neq1$, so $(\omega^k)^4 + (\omega^k)^3+(\omega^k)^2+\omega^k+1 = \frac{\omega^{5k}-1}{\omega^k-1} = 0$. Substituting $x = \omega^k$ in the identity gives
$$P(1) + \omega^kQ(1) + \omega^{2k}R(1) = 0\qquad(k=1,2,3,4).$$
So the polynomial $f(t) = P(1) + Q(1)\,t + R(1)\,t^2$, of degree at most $2$, has the four distinct roots $\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3,\omega^4$. A nonzero polynomial of degree $\le 2$ has at most $2$ roots, so $f$ is the zero polynomial: $P(1) = Q(1) = R(1) = 0$.

By the factor theorem, $P(1) = 0$ means $x - 1$ divides $P(x)$. ∎
